newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan bankers see reforms slowing economy.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan bankers see reforms slowing economy.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's IMF-inspired stabilisation package is likely to slow growth and raise interest rates, possibly without halting a drain of foreign reserves, bankers said on Wednesday.
"The measures will slow down the overall economy," Maqsood Ahmed, vice-president of the private Muslim Commercial Bank, told Reuters. "You can't expect to raise costs and achieve higher growth."

State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) governor Muhammad Yaqub on Tuesday unveiled tough measures aimed at averting any currency crisis and plug Pakistan's yawning budget and current account deficits.
He announced plans to narrow the budget gap by 40 billion rupees ($995 million) in 1996/97 (July-June) through spending cuts, extra taxes and a 10 percent rise in fuel prices.
The central bank has already devalued the rupee by 7.86 percent against the dollar and raised its key repurchase (repo) discount rate to 20 percent a year from 17 percent.

Ahmed said the package, designed to get the International Monetary Fund to resume stalled disbursements of a $600 million standby loan, would push up lending rates to the corporate sector, increase prices of raw material and fuel inflation.
"The government is sapping the viability of industries by raising their operational costs," he said.
Bankers said they doubted whether banks would respond to Yaqub's offer of 17 percent interest on foreign currency deposits placed with the central bank by November 28.
Yaqub said the move was meant to encourage forex inflows to shore up reserves that have tumbled to $756 million, excluding gold reserves of $800 million, from $831 million on October 3.
Salman Ahmed Siddiqui, a Treasury dealer at ABN AMRO bank, said the central bank actions smacked of desperation.
"Even after this (17 percent) offer and the devaluation, forex deposits, whether from institutions or individuals, would be hard to come by," he said.
Most institutions would be kept at bay by the threat of a possible cut in Pakistani credit ratings by Moody's Investors' Services, which sent a team to Islamabad this week.
The team left on Tuesday without saying whether its findings would result in a downgrade or not.
"Unless Pakistan re-estabilishes its credibility, very few international investor are likely to put their money into the country," Ahmed said.
Siddiqui said the higher repo rate would push up yields on government securities, raising the government's borrowing cost.
He said banks had been caught unawares at Tuesday's auction of six-month Federal bonds, which took place before news of the repo rate increase hit the market.
The banks would have submitted bids at much higher rates if they had known of the move beforehand, he added.

The SBP auctioned six-month federal bonds worth 5.165 billion rupees at an average yield of 14.27106 percent a year on Tuesday, receiving bids worth 5.165 million rupees against a pre-auction target of 13.065 billion rupees.
At the last auction on October 7, the bank auctioned short-term bonds worth 53.225 million rupees at a weighted average yield of 13.6406 percent. ($1 = 40.22 Rupees)
